items.title: A bottle with no inside
items.claim: A normal bottle has an inside and an outside, separated by the bottle wall. The Klein bottle has no inside. There is only one surface — what looks like 'inside' is connected to 'outside' through the surface itself.
items.prompt: How is the Klein bottle different from a regular surface?

options.text: It's non-orientable — there is no consistent way to assign 'outward normals'; a left-handed walker traversing it can come back as right-handed
It's actually two surfaces glued together
Klein bottles only exist in imagination

items.reveal:
Klein constructed the bottle as a 2D analogue of the Möbius strip — but closed. To build one in 3D, you must let the bottle 'pass through itself' (a fake self-intersection). Properly, it lives in 4-dimensional space, where it has no intersection.

In rigorous terms: the Klein bottle is a non-orientable, closed 2-manifold with Euler characteristic 0. It cannot be embedded in 3D Euclidean space without self-intersection.

The Möbius strip (Möbius, 1858) is a 2D example with boundary: cut one open and you get a long strip; cut it in half lengthwise and you get a single longer Möbius strip, not two.

Non-orientable surfaces matter in physics (some condensed matter systems behave like Möbius strips), engineering (conveyor belt design uses Möbius topology to wear evenly), and cosmology (toy models of non-orientable universes have been considered, though our universe seems to be orientable).
items.why: 3D objects have an obvious inside and outside. Topology shows some 2D surfaces don't — the apparently obvious 'inside/outside' distinction is a special feature of orientable manifolds.

items.title: Some quadratics never touch zero — and you can prove it in one step
items.claim: x^2 + 2x + 5: positive for every real x. The graph never reaches zero. You don't need calculus or graph-plotting — you can see this in one rearrangement.

options.text: Complete the square: x^2 + 2x + 5 = (x + 1)^2 + 4. The first term is non-negative; adding 4 means the whole expression is at least 4. Never zero
It cannot be proved without calculus

items.reveal:
For ax^2 + bx + c with a > 0, the discriminant b^2 - 4ac determines:
- Discriminant > 0: two real roots; graph crosses x-axis twice.
- Discriminant = 0: one repeated real root; graph touches x-axis.
- Discriminant < 0: no real roots; graph stays entirely above x-axis (if a > 0) or below (if a < 0).

x^2 + 2x + 5: a = 1, b = 2, c = 5. Discriminant = 4 - 20 = -16 < 0. No real roots.

Completing the square gives a stronger statement: the MINIMUM value of the quadratic. (x + 1)^2 + 4 has minimum 4 when x = -1. So x^2 + 2x + 5 is always at least 4.

General quadratic ax^2 + bx + c = a(x + b/(2a))^2 + (c - b^2/(4a)). Minimum value (for a > 0) is c - b^2/(4a) = -(b^2 - 4ac)/(4a) — same expression as the discriminant.

Applications:
- Optimisation: many minimisation problems reduce to completing the square.
- Inequality proofs: AM-GM and Cauchy-Schwarz often pivot on quadratic positivity.
- Definite matrices: a quadratic form x^T M x > 0 for all non-zero x means M is positive definite — central to optimisation and statistics.
items.why: Quadratics feel like they should always cross zero somewhere. Many don't. The discriminant settles which ones, and completing the square exposes the minimum directly — without calculus.

items.title: Computers compute sine by adding up polynomials
items.claim: Your calculator can't 'compute sine'. It computes a polynomial that approximates sine very accurately. Specifically, sin(x) = x - x^3/6 + x^5/120 - x^7/5040 + ... The Taylor series gives any function as a sum of polynomial terms.

options.text: Polynomials and sine are always equal
Any analytic function f(x) can be expressed as a power series sum of f^(n)(a) * (x-a)^n / n!; truncating to a few terms gives a polynomial approximation with rigorously bounded error near x = a
Only sine has a Taylor series

items.reveal:
Taylor series: f(x) = f(a) + f'(a)(x-a) + f''(a)(x-a)^2/2! + f'''(a)(x-a)^3/3! + ...

For analytic functions (most functions arising in physics and engineering), the series converges to f(x) within a radius of convergence around a.

Key examples around a = 0 (Maclaurin):
sin(x) = x - x^3/3! + x^5/5! - x^7/7! + ... (converges for all real x)
cos(x) = 1 - x^2/2! + x^4/4! - x^6/6! + ... (converges for all real x)
e^x = 1 + x + x^2/2! + x^3/3! + ... (converges for all real x)
ln(1+x) = x - x^2/2 + x^3/3 - ... (converges for |x| < 1)
1/(1-x) = 1 + x + x^2 + x^3 + ... (converges for |x| < 1, geometric)

For small x, truncating after a few terms gives good approximation. For sin(x), keeping x - x^3/6 gives error of about x^5/120; for x = 0.1, error ~ 10^(-8).

Calculators use TWO TRICKS:
1. Argument reduction: reduce sin(x) for large x to sin(x') where x' is in a small range, using periodicity and symmetries.
2. Polynomial approximation: minimax polynomials (Chebyshev-optimal) often beat Taylor for fixed precision.

Applications:
- Computer hardware (FPUs): implement transcendental functions via polynomial approximation.
- Numerical analysis: many algorithms (Newton-Raphson, Runge-Kutta) involve Taylor expansion.
- Physics: small-angle approximations (sin x ≈ x, cos x ≈ 1) are first-order Taylor.
- Perturbation theory in quantum mechanics: expansion of solutions around exactly-solvable cases.

Divergent Taylor series: some functions have Taylor series that converge only at a single point (formal series that don't represent the function). These appear in asymptotic analysis (Stirling's approximation, certain physics calculations).
items.why: Functions like sine seem 'analytical' or special. Computationally, they're polynomial approximations. The Taylor expansion is the practical universal interface between abstract functions and computers.
